CORE IDEA

This entire scene is one continuous shot.

Child Moss and Eli are already sparring with rough sticks.

Their fight should have real cause and effect. They are not simply standing opposite each other repeatedly hitting sticks together.

Every movement should have a reason:

one attacks
the other avoids or blocks
someone counters
one boy gives ground
they reset naturally
one notices an opening and tries to exploit it

The fight should still feel playful and improvised, especially as children, but there should always be a readable intention behind what they are doing.

As they gradually move left, the camera follows.

They pass behind the large tree.

The trunk completely obscures the frame.

When they emerge from the other side, they are suddenly their teen versions, continuing the exact same exchange seamlessly.

Then the camera gradually widens until their private game is revealed as something happening within the much larger settlement beneath the Wall.

FIGHT LANGUAGE
CHILD VERSION

Child Moss and Eli should fight like two boys who have done this game many times but have no formal training.

Not polished.

Not choreographed martial arts.

Not constant stick-on-stick contact.

Instead:

Moss tries an obvious swing toward Eli’s shoulder
Eli ducks or steps away rather than always blocking
Eli immediately tries to tap Moss’s side while he is exposed
Moss twists away and catches Eli’s stick once
they separate for half a beat
Moss feints high, then pokes low
Eli jumps back, laughing or breathing hard
one boy briefly gets the better angle and makes the other retreat

Their sticks should sometimes miss completely.

That is important.

The fight should feel like they are actually trying to touch one another with the sticks while avoiding being touched themselves.

TEEN VERSION

After the time transition, the same ritual has clearly developed.

They are now:

quicker
more economical
better at reading each other
less clumsy
more instinctive

But still not trained fighters.

Teen Moss might pressure more aggressively.

Teen Eli is slightly calmer and better at redirecting him.

Use simple believable actions:

a quick attack
parry
step around
counter
retreat
reset

No spins.

No acrobatics.

No elaborate weapon flourishes.

No endless rapid stick clashing.

He is taken by the hand into a world already packing itself away.
Between his mother on one side and his father on the other, he is led toward something impossibly large and impossible to understand.

Everyone around him treats the crossing as necessary.

Moss does not understand why.
He only knows he does not want to go.

His mother holds his hand.
His father stays close.

Together they step into darkness.
